hero.title: Test doubles
intro.0: How do you test code that depends on a clock, a random number, or the network - things that change every run or reach outside your program? You hand it a stand-in you control. This is what dependency injection was building towards: because a class receives its dependencies instead of creating them, a test can pass in a fake, a stub, or a spy.
task.1.title: Fake a shaky dependency
task.1.context:
When `Greeter` calls the real clock directly, your test is stuck with whatever time it actually is - it can pass this morning and fail tonight. Code that reaches for real things is hard to test.

**A fake** is a small class you write and inject in place of the real clock, so the test decides what it returns.

- Real clock: the hour changes, so the test passes in the morning and fails at night.
- Fake clock: `Hour()` always returns `9`, so the test gives the same result every run.
task.1.goal.0: Write a `FixedClock : IClock` whose `Hour()` always returns `9`.
task.1.goal.1: Main injects it and checks the greeting, so the output is PASS.
task.2.title: Feed it canned data
task.2.context:
To check `Total`, you need to know the price going in - but a real `IPriceFeed` reads a live price that moves, so you can't say what `Total(3)` should be.

**A stub** is a double that returns a value you choose, so you can set up one exact case.

- Real feed: an unpredictable live price, nothing you can check against.
- Stub feed: `Price()` returns `10`, so `Total(3)` is `30` - a number you can check.
task.2.goal.1: Main checks `Total(3)` is `30`, so the output is PASS.
task.3.title: Spy on the call
task.3.context:
`Signup.Register` tells the mailer to send a welcome email, then returns nothing. A test can't check a return value, and you don't want real mail going out - what you care about is whether it called the mailer at all.

**A spy** is a double that records how it was used, so you can confirm a call happened.

- Real mailer: sends actual mail and hands back nothing to inspect.
- Spy mailer: sets `WasCalled = true` on `Send()`, so the test can confirm the call.
task.3.goal.0: Write a `SpyMailer : IMailer` with a public `bool WasCalled` that `Send()` sets to `true`.
task.3.goal.1: Main registers a user and checks the mailer was called, so the output is PASS.
task.4.title: Test doubles - recap
task.4.context: A double stands in for a real dependency so a test is fast, repeatable and under your control.
task.4.summaryIntro: Real dependencies - a clock, a live feed, a mailer - give a different answer each run or reach outside your program. A double is a stand-in you pass in during a test. You can pass one in because the class receives its dependencies through injection, against an interface rather than a concrete type - the payoff of that earlier work.
task.4.summaryItems.0.title: Fake -
task.4.summaryItems.0.text: a plain working stand-in with fixed behaviour: a clock that is always `9`, so the test repeats.
task.4.summaryItems.1.title: Stub -
task.4.summaryItems.1.text: returns a value you chose, so you arrange one exact case and can predict the result.
task.4.summaryItems.2.title: Spy -
task.4.summaryItems.2.text: remembers how it was used, so you can confirm a call happened when there is no return value to check.
task.4.summaryClose: Next: testable by design - the habits that make code easy to test are the habits behind SOLID.
